@@@ USER
How do I find the biggest files in a folder (and all its subfolders) on Windows using PowerShell? I want name and size in KB.
@@@ ASSISTANT
List all files recursively, sort by `Length` (the size in bytes), take the first few, and calculate the size column.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File |
  Sort-Object Length -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 10 Name, @{Name='SizeKB'; Expression={[math]::Round($_.Length / 1KB, 1)}} |
  Format-Table -AutoSize
```

Example output for a folder with three files:

```
Name  SizeKB
----  ------
b.bin      5
c.log      3
a.txt      1
```

How it works:
- `-Recurse` goes into all subfolders; `-File` skips folders.
- `Sort-Object Length -Descending` puts the biggest first.
- `@{Name=...; Expression={...}}` is a **calculated property**: a new column made from a script block, where `$_` is the current file. `1KB` is built into PowerShell (1024).
- Use `-First 10` to keep the list short. For huge folders add `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` after `-File` to hide "access denied" messages.
- To see where each file lives, add `Directory` to the `Select-Object` list.
- The cmd.exe way is much weaker: `dir /s /o-s` sorts only inside each folder.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
In PowerShell, how do I search for the text TODO inside all .py files of a project and see file name, line number and the line?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Pipe the files into `Select-String`. It is the PowerShell version of `grep`, and it returns objects, so you can pick the columns you want.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.py |
  Select-String -Pattern 'TODO' |
  Select-Object Filename, LineNumber, Line |
  Format-Table -AutoSize
```

Example output (two Python files, plus a `notes.txt` that is ignored because of the filter):

```
Filename LineNumber Line
-------- ---------- ----
app.py            2 # TODO: handle errors
util.py           2     return 1  # todo later
util.py           3 # TODO: tests
```

Notes:
- `Select-String` ignores upper/lower case by default, so `# todo later` is found too. Add `-CaseSensitive` if you want an exact match.
- `-Pattern` is a **regular expression**. For a plain text with special characters use `-SimpleMatch`.
- `-Filter *.py` is faster than `-Include`, because the file system does the filtering.
- Skip big folders such as `node_modules` and `.git`: add `| Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch 'node_modules|\\.git\\' }` after `Get-ChildItem`.
- On Linux and macOS the same job is `grep -rn "TODO" --include="*.py" .`
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I rename many files at once in PowerShell, for example change all .jpeg files to .jpg? I want to preview first.
@@@ ASSISTANT
`Rename-Item` accepts a **script block** for `-NewName`, so the new name can be calculated for each file. The `-WhatIf` switch shows what would happen without changing anything. Always run it first.

```powershell
# 1. preview only: nothing is renamed
Get-ChildItem -Filter *.jpeg | Rename-Item -NewName { $_.BaseName + '.jpg' } -WhatIf

# 2. do it
Get-ChildItem -Filter *.jpeg | Rename-Item -NewName { $_.BaseName + '.jpg' }

# 3. check
(Get-ChildItem).Name
```

Output (the folder here is `C:\work`):

```
What if: Performing the operation "Rename File" on target "Item: C:\work\a.jpeg Destination: C:\work\a.jpg".
What if: Performing the operation "Rename File" on target "Item: C:\work\b.jpeg Destination: C:\work\b.jpg".
a.jpg
b.jpg
keep.png
```

Notes:
- `$_.BaseName` is the name without the extension, so `photo.jpeg` becomes `photo.jpg`.
- The same idea works for other changes: add a prefix with `'2026_' + $_.Name`, make lowercase with `$_.Name.ToLower()`, replace text with `$_.Name -replace ' ', '_'`.
- Add `-Recurse` to `Get-ChildItem` to include subfolders.
- If two files would get the same new name, PowerShell stops with an error for that file instead of overwriting.
- `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm` work with most commands that change something (`Remove-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Stop-Process`). Use them whenever you are not sure.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
I have a sales.csv with the columns date, region, amount. How do I get the number of orders and the total amount per region in PowerShell, biggest total first?

```
date,region,amount
2026-11-01,North,120.50
2026-11-01,South,80
2026-11-02,North,60
2026-11-02,East,200
2026-11-03,South,45.25
```
@@@ ASSISTANT
`Import-Csv` turns every row into an object with properties named like the columns. Group by region, build one summary object per group, then sort.

```powershell
Import-Csv sales.csv |
  Group-Object region |
  ForEach-Object {
    [pscustomobject]@{
      Region = $_.Name
      Orders = $_.Count
      Total  = ($_.Group | ForEach-Object { [decimal]$_.amount } | Measure-Object -Sum).Sum
    }
  } |
  Sort-Object Total -Descending |
  Format-Table -AutoSize
```

Output:

```
Region Orders  Total
------ ------  -----
East        1    200
North       2  180.5
South       2 125.25
```

Why each step is needed:
- All values from `Import-Csv` are **text**. `[decimal]$_.amount` converts them to numbers. Without the conversion, sorting would be alphabetical ("80" after "200") and sums can fail.
- `Group-Object` gives each group a `Name` (the region), a `Count` and the `Group` (the rows).
- `[pscustomobject]@{...}` creates a new row object. This works in every PowerShell version; do not use `Measure-Object { script }` because only PowerShell 7 supports that.
- To save the result use `Export-Csv summary.csv -NoTypeInformation` instead of `Format-Table` (which is only for display).
@@@ END

@@@ USER
My app.log has lines like "2026-11-12 09:40:12 ERROR db timeout". In PowerShell, how do I count the ERROR lines per hour?

```
2026-11-12 09:15:01 INFO  started
2026-11-12 09:40:12 ERROR db timeout
2026-11-12 10:02:55 ERROR db timeout
2026-11-12 10:03:10 WARN  slow query
2026-11-12 10:59:59 ERROR disk full
2026-11-12 12:00:00 INFO  heartbeat
```
@@@ ASSISTANT
Keep only the lines with ` ERROR `, cut the hour out of the time column, then count the groups.

```powershell
Get-Content app.log |
  Where-Object { $_ -match ' ERROR ' } |
  ForEach-Object { ($_ -split ' ')[1].Substring(0, 2) } |
  Group-Object |
  Sort-Object Name |
  ForEach-Object { '{0}:00  {1} error(s)' -f $_.Name, $_.Count }
```

Output:

```
09:00  1 error(s)
10:00  2 error(s)
```

Explanation:
- `$_ -split ' '` cuts a line at spaces; element `[1]` is the time `09:40:12`; `Substring(0, 2)` is the hour.
- `Group-Object` without a property groups equal strings, and gives each group a `Count`.
- `-f` is the format operator: `{0}` and `{1}` are replaced by the arguments.
- Hours without errors do not appear (12:00 is missing). Add them yourself if you need a complete table.
- A log with a different format needs a different cut. A regular expression is more robust: `if ($_ -match '^\S+ (\d\d):') { $Matches[1] }`.
- For very large logs, `Get-Content -ReadCount 1000` or `Select-String` is faster than reading line by line.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Write a PowerShell function that backs up a folder into .\backups with today's date in the name. It must check that the folder exists and print a clear message when copying fails.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Use an **advanced function** (`[CmdletBinding()]`) with a typed, validated parameter, and a `try/catch` around the operations. `-ErrorAction Stop` is important: many cmdlets only print a **non-terminating** error, which `catch` cannot see, unless you turn it into a terminating one.

```powershell
function Backup-Folder {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateScript({ Test-Path $_ -PathType Container })]
        [string]$Source,

        [string]$Destination = '.\backups'
    )

    $stamp  = Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd'
    $target = Join-Path $Destination ((Split-Path $Source -Leaf) + "-$stamp")

    try {
        New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Destination -Force -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
        Copy-Item -Path $Source -Destination $target -Recurse -ErrorAction Stop
        Write-Host "Backed up to $target"
    }
    catch {
        Write-Error "Backup failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    }
}

Backup-Folder -Source .\project
Backup-Folder -Source .\missing
```

Output (run on 13 November 2026):

```
Backed up to .\backups\project-20261113
Backup-Folder : Cannot validate argument on parameter 'Source'. The " Test-Path $_ -PathType Container " validation script for the argument with value ".\missing" did not return a result of True. Determine why the validation script failed, and then try the command again.
```

The folder `.\backups\project-20261113` now contains a copy of everything in `project`.

Details:
- `[Parameter(Mandatory)]` asks for the value if you forget it. `[ValidateScript]` rejects a folder that does not exist **before** the function body runs, with a clear message.
- `Join-Path` and `Split-Path -Leaf` build the target name safely, with the right slashes and without string cutting.
- Running the backup twice on the same day gives an error, because the target already exists. Add the time to the stamp (`yyyyMMdd-HHmmss`) if you want several backups per day.
- To run it every night use Task Scheduler with `powershell.exe -NoProfile -File C:\scripts\backup.ps1`.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How do I see how much space each top-level folder uses in PowerShell, biggest first, in MB?
@@@ ASSISTANT
PowerShell has no single command like `du`. Loop over the folders, add up the sizes of all files inside each one, and create one row per folder.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Directory | ForEach-Object {
    $bytes = (Get-ChildItem $_.FullName -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
              Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum
    [pscustomobject]@{ Folder = $_.Name; SizeMB = [math]::Round($bytes / 1MB, 2) }
} | Sort-Object SizeMB -Descending | Format-Table -AutoSize
```

Output for a folder `docs` with one 1 MB file and a folder `media` with 3 MB and 1 MB files:

```
Folder SizeMB
------ ------
media       4
docs        1
```

Notes:
- `Measure-Object Length -Sum` adds the `Length` of every file; the `.Sum` property is the total in bytes.
- `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` hides "access denied" messages for folders you cannot read (the totals then miss those files).
- An empty folder has no files, so `.Sum` is empty and the size shows as 0.
- This reads every file entry, so it takes a while on a big drive (for example `C:\Users`). For a quick look at where the space went, a tool such as WinDirStat or TreeSize is faster.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
How can I find duplicate files in a folder with PowerShell? Files with the same content, even when the names differ.
@@@ ASSISTANT
Calculate a **hash** of the content of every file. Files with the same hash have the same content, whatever their names are.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -File |
  Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 |
  Group-Object Hash |
  Where-Object Count -gt 1 |
  ForEach-Object { ($_.Group.Path | Split-Path -Leaf) -join '  =  ' }
```

Output for a folder with `a.txt` and `copy_of_a.txt` (same text) and `b.txt` (different text):

```
a.txt  =  copy_of_a.txt
```

Explanation:
- `Get-FileHash` returns an object with `Hash` and `Path` for each file.
- `Group-Object Hash` puts files with the same hash together; `Where-Object Count -gt 1` keeps only the groups with more than one file.
- Add `-Recurse` to `Get-ChildItem` to look in subfolders too.
- Hashing reads the whole file, so on big folders first group by `Length` (files with different sizes cannot be equal) and hash only the groups that have more than one file.
- **Check before you delete.** List the duplicates, look at them, then remove the ones you do not need with `Remove-Item -WhatIf` first.
@@@ END

@@@ USER
Port 3000 is already in use on my Windows PC and my dev server will not start. How do I find which program uses it and stop it?
@@@ ASSISTANT
Ask Windows which process **owns** the connection that listens on that port, then look up the process by its ID.

```powershell
# 1. which process listens on port 3000?
$conn = Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
$conn | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

# 2. what is it?
Get-Process -Id $conn.OwningProcess | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path

# 3. stop it (only if it is really not needed)
Stop-Process -Id $conn.OwningProcess
```

The output depends on your computer. It looks like this when a Node server is running:

```
LocalAddress LocalPort OwningProcess
------------ --------- -------------
::                3000         14212

   Id ProcessName Path
   -- ----------- ----
14212 node        C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe
```

The old way with cmd.exe works on every Windows version:

```
netstat -ano | findstr :3000
taskkill /PID 14212 /F
```

Notes:
- If step 1 prints nothing, nothing listens on the port. The error then comes from something else, such as a firewall rule or a port that Windows reserved (check with `netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp`).
- Look at the process name before you stop it. An old `node` that you started yourself is fine to stop; a system process or your database is not.
- `Stop-Process` without `-Force` asks the program to end in the normal way when it can. Use `-Force` only when it does not react.
- The easier long-term fix is to start the dev server on another port, for example `npm run dev -- --port 3001`.
@@@ END
